how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response includes a 'retention_days' or equivalent integer field indicating the configured retention window.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse the snapshot task configuration file to extract the retention period value directly from the stored task definition.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line such as 'retention_days=30' or 'max_snapshots=10' is present, from which retention duration can be calculated.

option_description: Indicates whether snapshot data is written to the same underlying volume or disk pool as the source data it is meant to protect, or whether it is isolated on a separate volume, RAID group, or offsite destination.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers snapshot_and_backup_misconfiguration when snapshots_enabled is true and snapshot_stored_on_same_volume is true. Co-location of snapshots and source data means a ransomware attack that encrypts the source volume will also encrypt or delete the snapshots stored on that same volume—entirely defeating their recovery purpose. Disk failure events similarly destroy both the live data and its snapshots simultaneously. Isolation is the security control; same-volume storage is the default on many NAS platforms unless explicitly reconfigured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the snapshot destination configuration in the NAS management interface. On Synology DSM go to Storage Manager > Snapshot Replication and check whether the snapshot destination is the same storage pool as the source share or a different one. On QNAP QTS go to Storage & Snapshots > Snapshot > Snapshot Manager and verify whether snapshot storage is allocated on a separate volume or the same volume tier.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Storage Manager > Snapshot Replication > [task] > Destination (Synology) | Storage & Snapshots > Snapshot > Snapshot Manager > [volume] > Snapshot Storage (QNAP)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Destination shows a different volume name, pool ID, or offsite/cloud location than the source volume being protected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: SSH into the NAS and enumerate snapshot storage mappings to determine if any snapshot job writes to the same underlying block device or volume group as its source.
how_to_obtain.command: btrfs subvolume list / | grep -i snapshot ; df -h | grep -i snap ; synoschedtask --get | grep -E 'src_share|dst_share|destination'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Source and destination volume identifiers differ; if they reference the same device node or pool name, snapshots are co-located.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the snapshot task details via the NAS API to retrieve source and destination volume identifiers and compare them to determine co-location.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response shows distinct source_volume and destination_volume identifiers, or destination_type indicating 'remote' or 'offsite'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the storage administrator responsible for the NAS and ask whether snapshot replication to a separate physical volume, offsite NAS, or cloud object storage has been deliberately configured as part of the backup design. Review any documented backup architecture diagrams.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Administrator confirms and can demonstrate that snapshots replicate to a physically separate volume or remote system, with documentation supporting that architecture decision.

option_description: Counts the total number of local user accounts on the NAS device that have been granted administrator-level or root-equivalent privileges, excluding domain or LDAP-sourced accounts.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers excessive_privileged_local_accounts when local_admin_account_count exceeds 2, reflecting that legitimate operations typically require at most one named primary admin and one break-glass emergency account. Each additional local admin account expands the blast radius: if any single account's credentials are compromised via phishing, credential stuffing, or password reuse, the attacker gains full NAS administrative access. More accounts also increase the probability that at least one account has a weak or unchanged password, particularly if the NAS was deployed with vendor default secondary accounts still present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Access the NAS user management interface and filter for accounts with administrator roles. On Synology DSM go to Control Panel > User & Group and sort by group membership, identifying all accounts in the 'administrators' group. On QNAP QTS go to Control Panel > Privilege > Users and filter by role to identify admin-role accounts.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Control Panel > User & Group > User list (Synology) | Control Panel > Privilege > Users > filter by Administrator role (QNAP)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of local accounts is shown; count all entries with 'Administrator' group membership or admin role assigned. Record the total count.

how_to_obtain.instruction: SSH into the NAS and query the local user database to enumerate all accounts with UID 0 or membership in the admin/wheel group.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists all accounts with UID 0 (root-equivalent) and all accounts in administrative groups. Count the unique entries to get local_admin_account_count.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the NAS management API to enumerate local users and their group memberships, filtering for administrator group membership.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response contains a 'users' array; the count of entries in that array represents local_admin_account_count.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the NAS group configuration file directly to count members of the administrators or admin group without relying on the management UI.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '^admin' /etc/group ; getent group administrators 2>/dev/null || getent group admin 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows the administrators group entry with a comma-separated member list; count the members for local_admin_account_count.

option_description: Indicates whether any accounts used by automated processes, backup jobs, application integrations, or scheduled scripts have been granted full administrator-level privileges on the NAS rather than operating with scoped least-privilege permissions.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers excessive_privileged_local_accounts when service_accounts_with_admin_role is true, because service accounts are high-value credential targets: they are frequently embedded in scripts, configuration files, or automation platforms where they may be exposed. If such an account also holds administrator privileges on the NAS, a credential exposure in any connected system grants an attacker complete NAS control, including the ability to disable snapshots, modify share permissions, delete data, and disable audit logging—all with the service account's credentials. Least-privilege service account design is a critical mitigating control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the NAS user management interface, enumerate all local accounts and cross-reference each account's role with its apparent purpose. Accounts with names indicating service usage (e.g., 'backup_svc', 'veeam', 'monitoring', 'replication') that appear in the administrators group should be flagged. On Synology DSM check Control Panel > User & Group > Users, then click each service-named account to view group membership.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Control Panel > User & Group > Users > [each service account] > Groups tab (Synology) | Control Panel > Privilege > Users > [service account] > Edit Permissions (QNAP)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service-named accounts do NOT appear in the 'administrators' group. If any do, service_accounts_with_admin_role is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: SSH into the NAS and compare the admin group membership list against a pattern-matched list of known service account naming conventions to identify service accounts with elevated privileges.
how_to_obtain.command: for user in $(getent group admin administrators 2>/dev/null | cut -d: -f4 | tr ',' ' '); do echo $user; done | grep -iE 'svc|service|backup|monitor|replicate|sync|veeam|commvault|zabbix|nagios|automation|app'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output means no pattern-matched service accounts hold admin roles. Any output indicates service_accounts_with_admin_role is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the NAS administrator and any application team members who have configured integrations with the NAS (backup software, monitoring agents, cloud sync tools). Ask explicitly what credentials each integration uses and what privilege level those accounts hold.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All integration and automation accounts are confirmed to use dedicated non-admin accounts with only the specific permissions required for their function (e.g., read-only for monitoring, write to specific share for backup).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review NAS authentication logs and admin action logs to identify whether any service-named accounts have performed administrative operations such as configuration changes, user management, or share ACL modifications, which would indicate admin-level access is being actively used.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No administrative action log entries attributed to service-named accounts. Presence of such entries confirms admin role usage.

option_description: Indicates whether two or more personnel or automated systems authenticate to the NAS using identical shared administrative credentials—such as a generic 'admin' or 'nasadmin' account—rather than each administrator having a uniquely named, individually accountable account.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers excessive_privileged_local_accounts when shared_admin_credentials_in_use is true, because shared credentials eliminate individual accountability: if the shared admin account performs a destructive action or is used by an attacker, audit logs cannot attribute the activity to a specific person, defeating forensic investigation and non-repudiation requirements. Additionally, shared passwords are statistically more likely to be exposed because they must be communicated across multiple people and may be documented in shared runbooks, ticket systems, or chat logs. Password rotation also becomes organizationally difficult, leading to long-lived weak credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview all staff members with NAS administrative access and ask whether each person has their own uniquely named administrator account or whether they share a common admin account. Review IT onboarding runbooks, team wikis, and password manager vaults for entries indicating a shared 'admin' or 'nasadmin' credential is distributed to multiple staff.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each administrator confirms they use a personally named account (e.g., 'jsmith_admin') rather than a shared generic account. Absence of a shared credential entry in documentation supports shared_admin_credentials_in_use = false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review admin account naming conventions in the NAS user management interface. Accounts with generic names such as 'admin', 'administrator', 'nas_admin', 'root', or 'sysadmin' with no individual name association are indicators of shared credential use. Check the number of admin accounts against the known number of administrators: if there are 5 admins but only 1 admin account, sharing is almost certain.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Control Panel > User & Group > Users > filter by administrators group (Synology) | Control Panel > Privilege > Users (QNAP)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The count of uniquely named admin accounts equals the count of individuals with administrative responsibilities. Generic account names are absent or exist only as disabled break-glass accounts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Analyze NAS authentication logs for the admin account to detect simultaneous or near-simultaneous login sessions from multiple distinct source IP addresses, which would indicate multiple individuals sharing the same account credentials.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Login entries for the generic admin account show logins from only one source IP at a time. Multiple distinct source IPs authenticating as 'admin' within the same business day strongly suggests shared credential use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the NAS audit log API for recent authentication events attributed to generic admin account names and correlate the source IP addresses across multiple sessions to identify multi-user sharing patterns.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response shows authentication events for the generic 'admin' account; if source IPs vary across events from multiple days or hours, this is indicative of credential sharing.

option_description: Controls whether configuration files that store service credentials — including backup job configs, LDAP bind passwords, and replication credentials — are encrypted at rest on the appliance filesystem rather than written as human-readable plaintext.
security_impact: The Rego rule `hardcoded_or_plaintext_stored_credentials` fires when `credential_files_encrypted` is false or absent, triggering the exposure. Plaintext credential files on a NAS filesystem are trivially readable by any process or user with filesystem access, enabling lateral movement by extracting LDAP bind passwords, backup service accounts, or replication keys from a single compromised shell session.

how_to_obtain.instruction: SSH into the NAS appliance and inspect common credential-bearing configuration files for readable password fields.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: values appear as encrypted ciphertext strings (e.g., ENC[AES256,...] or $6$... style hashes). Insecure result: visible plaintext strings such as 'password=MyP@ssw0rd' or 'bindpw secretvalue'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the LDAP client configuration file directly for plaintext bind password fields.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: field is absent, blank, or references an external secrets provider. Insecure result: 'bindpw <plaintext_password>' visible in the file.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check file permissions and content of replication configuration files to verify they are not world-readable and do not store plaintext credentials.
how_to_obtain.command: find /etc /opt /var/lib -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.cfg' -o -name '*.ini' 2>/dev/null | xargs ls -la 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^d'; find /etc /opt -name '*.conf' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -li 'password\|passwd\|secret' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: no world-readable config files containing password fields, or all password fields show encrypted values.

option_description: Indicates whether shell scripts, Python scripts, or other automation scripts present on the appliance filesystem embed usernames, passwords, API tokens, or other secrets directly in plaintext within the script body rather than sourcing them from a secrets store or environment variable.
security_impact: The Rego rule `hardcoded_or_plaintext_stored_credentials` triggers when `scripts_contain_hardcoded_credentials` is true, raising the exposure regardless of whether config files are encrypted. Hardcoded credentials in scripts are especially dangerous on NAS appliances because cron directories and /usr/local/bin are often writable by service accounts, meaning an attacker who reads a backup or replication script immediately obtains valid credentials for downstream systems.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan all scripts in common NAS automation directories for patterns that indicate embedded credentials.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: no output, or matched lines reference environment variables (e.g., PASSWORD=$VAULT_SECRET) or external credential files. Insecure result: lines such as 'PASSWORD=Backup123!' or 'rsync -e ssh user:MyPass@host'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search specifically for credentials passed inline to command-line tools such as rsync, mysql, curl, or smbclient within scripts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: no matches or all matches use variable substitution. Insecure result: literal credential values embedded in command arguments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all executable scripts under relevant directories and inspect those modified recently for newly introduced credentials.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: no recently modified scripts contain credential-related keywords. Insecure result: list of scripts that embed credentials and have been recently changed.

typical_values: true (common in legacy NAS deployments with hand-crafted backup scripts)

option_description: Describes the mechanism the NAS appliance uses to store service credentials such as LDAP bind passwords, backup account passwords, and replication credentials. Valid values are plaintext_file (credentials in readable text), encrypted_file (credentials encrypted on disk), secrets_manager (credentials fetched from an external vault), hashed (one-way hash, applicable mainly to local auth passwords), or unknown (mechanism cannot be determined).
security_impact: The Rego rule `hardcoded_or_plaintext_stored_credentials` fires explicitly when `credential_store_type == 'plaintext_file'`, making this attribute a direct trigger for the exposure. A plaintext_file store means any filesystem read — whether by an authenticated attacker, a malicious process, or a forensic image of a stolen drive — yields usable credentials for backup targets, directory services, and replication partners.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the primary NAS credential storage files and determine whether values are human-readable plaintext, ciphertext blobs, or references to external stores.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/shadow 2>/dev/null | head -5; cat /etc/ldap.conf 2>/dev/null | grep -i pass; cat /etc/backup.conf 2>/dev/null; ls -la /etc/credentials* /etc/.secrets* /opt/*/conf/*.conf 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: encrypted_file: values show as ciphertext prefixes such as ENC[ or {ENC}. secrets_manager: values contain vault:// URIs or references to HashiCorp Vault / AWS Secrets Manager endpoints. hashed: values begin with $6$ or $2b$ (shadow format). plaintext_file: raw human-readable strings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the NAS management web interface and navigate to the credential or integration settings page to review how stored passwords are displayed.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management UI → System → Integrations (or Directory Services) → LDAP / Backup → Credential Storage. Check whether the password field shows masked ciphertext, a secrets-manager reference, or a readable password hint that suggests plaintext storage.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: password fields show '***' with a note indicating encrypted or vault-backed storage. Insecure result: password field shows a recoverable or displayable value indicating plaintext_file storage.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the NAS vendor API to retrieve configuration objects and inspect the credential representation in the response payload.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: password field returns a masked value, a KMS key ARN, or a secrets-manager path. Insecure result: password field returns the literal credential value.

typical_values: unknown (default when appliance cannot be directly inspected)

option_description: Captures the client or host restriction field from the NFS export configuration — the value in /etc/exports (or equivalent) that determines which hosts are permitted to mount the exported filesystem. Examples range from '*' (any host) and broad CIDR ranges to specific IP addresses or hostnames.
security_impact: The Rego rule `unrestricted_nfs_exports_by_host` fires when the specification is '*', contains a wildcard, or matches CIDR masks of /16 or broader (regex patterns in the policy), directly producing the exposure. Overly broad host specifications mean any host on a reachable network can mount the NFS share without further authentication, enabling mass data exfiltration or ransomware encryption of shared volumes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the /etc/exports file and extract the host/client specification field from each export line.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: entries show specific IPs or hostnames such as '/data 10.10.5.20(rw,sync,root_squash)'. Insecure result: entries show '/data *(rw)' or '/data 10.0.0.0/8(rw)'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nfsstat or exportfs to display currently active exports and their client specifications.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists each exported path with its client specification and options. Insecure result: client field shows '*' or a CIDR with prefix /16 or shorter.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the NFS Shares section in the NAS management interface to review each share's allowed hosts setting.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management UI → Shared Folders → NFS → [Select share] → Allowed Hosts / Client Specification. Review each export entry for wildcard or broad range values.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: each share lists specific trusted IP addresses or hostnames. Insecure result: shares list '*' or a subnet such as '0.0.0.0/0' or '10.0.0.0/8'.

option_description: Indicates whether the NFS export is configured with the `no_root_squash` option, which causes the NFS server to honour root-level UIDs from mounting clients rather than remapping them to the anonymous user (nobody). When enabled, a client mounting the share as root retains root-equivalent access on the server-side filesystem.
security_impact: The Rego rule `unrestricted_nfs_exports_by_host` has a combined condition that fires when `export_host_specification` contains a wildcard AND `export_options_include_no_root_squash` is true, compounding the exposure. Even without the wildcard combination, no_root_squash allows any client permitted to mount the share — particularly one already compromised — to read, overwrite, or delete any file on the exported filesystem regardless of POSIX ownership, enabling full data exfiltration or ransomware deployment with root access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect /etc/exports for the no_root_squash option on each export line.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: no output (option absent, meaning root_squash is in effect by default). Insecure result: one or more export lines include 'no_root_squash'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use exportfs to display verbose active export options and filter for no_root_squash.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: no output. Insecure result: lines listing the exported path followed by options including 'no_root_squash'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review NFS share advanced options in the management UI to check root squashing settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management UI → Shared Folders → NFS → [Select share] → Advanced Options → Root Squash. Verify that 'Root Squash' or 'Squash Root' is enabled (not 'No Root Squash').
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: 'Root Squash' is selected or enabled. Insecure result: 'No Root Squash' option is selected.

typical_values: true (explicitly set for legacy application compatibility, insecure)

option_description: Controls whether multi-factor authentication is mandatory for every administrative login to the NAS management interface (web UI or API). When true, successful login requires both a valid password and a second factor; when false, password-only authentication is accepted.
security_impact: The Rego rule `missing_multi_factor_authentication_on_management` fires when `mfa_enforced_on_management_ui` is false or absent, directly triggering the exposure. NAS management interfaces that accept password-only authentication are vulnerable to credential stuffing attacks (using breached password databases), phishing-captured passwords, or brute-force — especially when exposed on internal networks accessible from lateral movement paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the NAS management portal and navigate to the account security or authentication policy settings to check MFA enforcement status.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management UI → Control Panel → Security → Account (or 2-Step Verification) → Enforce 2-Step Verification for administrators. Check whether the enforcement toggle is enabled and applies to all admin accounts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: MFA enforcement toggle is 'On' and scoped to 'All users' or 'Administrators'. Insecure result: toggle is 'Off' or set to 'Optional'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the NAS management API for the MFA enforcement policy configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: response contains 'enforced': true or 'mfa_required': true. Insecure result: field is false, null, or absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the NAS administrator and request documented evidence (screenshot or policy export) confirming MFA is enforced for all admin accounts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: administrator can demonstrate that login without a second factor fails for admin accounts. Insecure result: administrator confirms MFA is optional or only applied to specific accounts.

typical_values: false (default on most NAS appliances out of the box)

option_description: Lists all authentication methods currently enabled for the NAS management interface login flow, such as 'password', 'totp', 'hardware_token', 'push_notification', 'ldap', or 'saml_mfa'. The presence or absence of MFA-capable methods in this list determines whether strong authentication is technically possible regardless of enforcement policy.
security_impact: The Rego rule `missing_multi_factor_authentication_on_management` has a second condition that fires when none of 'totp', 'hardware_token', 'push_notification', or 'saml_mfa' appear in `authentication_methods_enabled` — meaning even if MFA enforcement is intended, no MFA method is technically available. A management interface limited to password and ldap methods cannot enforce MFA, leaving the appliance exposed to single-factor credential attacks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the authentication or two-factor verification settings in the management portal and document all listed and enabled login methods.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management UI → Control Panel → Security → 2-Step Verification (or Authentication Settings). List all methods shown as 'Enabled' or 'Active', including TOTP apps, hardware keys (FIDO2/YubiKey), push notification services, and SAML providers.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: at least one of TOTP, hardware_token, push_notification, or SAML MFA is listed as enabled. Insecure result: only 'password' and optionally 'ldap' are enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the authentication methods configuration via the NAS REST API.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: JSON array contains objects with method names including 'totp', 'hardware_token', 'push_notification', or 'saml_mfa' with enabled status true. Insecure result: only 'password' or 'ldap' methods appear.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On appliances that write authentication configuration to disk, inspect the auth configuration file for enabled method entries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: configuration entries show enabled MFA methods. Insecure result: only password or ldap entries are present.

option_description: Lists the network interface names (or identifiers) to which storage protocols — SMB, NFS, iSCSI, AFP, FTP — are bound and listening. Should contain only trusted internal VLAN interface names; the presence of 'all', 'dmz', 'internet-facing', or equivalent untrusted interface designators directly indicates an over-exposed attack surface.
security_impact: The Rego rule `network_binding_to_untrusted_interfaces` fires when 'all', 'dmz', or 'internet-facing' appear in `storage_protocol_bound_interfaces`, producing the network exposure finding. Storage protocols bound to DMZ or all-interfaces configurations allow any host on those segments — including internet-sourced traffic — to interact with SMB, NFS, or iSCSI ports, making the NAS reachable for ransomware campaigns, credential brute-force, and data exfiltration without requiring internal network access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check which network interfaces each storage protocol is listening on using ss or netstat.
how_to_obtain.command: ss -tlnp | grep -E ':445|:139|:2049|:3260|:21|:548'; ip addr show; cat /proc/net/if_inet6 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $5}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: storage protocol ports (445, 139, 2049, 3260, 21, 548) bind to specific trusted VLAN IP addresses only. Insecure result: ports show '0.0.0.0' or ':::' indicating all-interface binding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect SMB and NFS configuration files for interface binding directives.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: smb.conf shows 'interfaces = eth1 10.10.5.0/24' and 'bind interfaces only = yes'. Insecure result: no binding directives present (defaults to all interfaces) or explicit '0.0.0.0' entries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network binding settings for each storage protocol in the NAS management interface.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Management UI → Control Panel → File Services → [SMB / NFS / iSCSI / FTP] → Network Interface. For each enabled protocol, verify that only internal VLAN interface names are selected and that 'All Interfaces' is not chosen.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: each protocol shows specific trusted VLAN interface names such as 'LAN1 (10.10.5.0/24)'. Insecure result: 'All Interfaces' is selected or untrusted interfaces such as 'DMZ' or 'WAN' are included.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Conduct an external or DMZ-perspective port scan to verify that storage protocol ports are not reachable from untrusted network segments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secure result: all storage protocol ports show as filtered or closed from the DMZ or external scan source. Insecure result: one or more ports show as open from the untrusted segment.

typical_values: ["eth0", "eth1"] (interface-specific but requires validation of VLAN trust)

option_description: Controls whether the NAS management interface (web UI, SSH, SNMP) listens on all available network interfaces (0.0.0.0 or ::) rather than being restricted to a specific trusted management VLAN adapter. When bound to all interfaces, any network segment reachable to the appliance can initiate management-plane connections.
security_impact: The Rego rule network_binding_to_untrusted_interfaces fires when management_interface_bound_to_all is true AND untrusted_interface_types_present is non-empty. This combination means the management UI is reachable from DMZ, guest, or internet-facing segments, dramatically expanding the attack surface for credential attacks, CVE exploitation against the management daemon, and lateral movement pivoting through the storage appliance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: SSH into the NAS and run ss or netstat to identify which addresses the management service is bound to. Look for the web UI port (5000/5001 on Synology, 8080/443 on QNAP, 80/443 generic) and check whether the local address column shows 0.0.0.0 or *.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-vulnerable result shows a specific IP (e.g., 192.168.10.5:5001) rather than 0.0.0.0:5001 or :::5001, indicating the service is bound to one interface only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the NAS management daemon configuration file for the listen address directive. On Synology DSM check /etc/nginx/app.d/ or /usr/syno/etc/. On QNAP inspect /etc/config/apache/ or the qthttpd configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Listen directives should reference a specific management IP rather than 0.0.0.0 or all. Any 0.0.0.0 entry confirms the attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Synology DSM navigate to Control Panel > Network > Network Interface, then cross-reference with Control Panel > Security > Firewall to see which interfaces management ports are exposed on. On QNAP go to System > Network > TCP/IP and review the service binding settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Synology: Control Panel > Security > Firewall | QNAP: Control Panel > System > Security > Allow/Deny List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Management services should explicitly list only the management VLAN interface IP. Absence of interface binding configuration implies all-interface binding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host on an untrusted VLAN (e.g., a guest or DMZ segment), attempt to reach the NAS management port. A successful TCP connection confirms the interface is bound to all adapters.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A hardened NAS should return connection refused or timeout from untrusted segments. A successful connect means management_interface_bound_to_all is effectively true.

option_description: An array listing the network interface classifications present on the NAS device that are considered untrusted or outside the storage VLAN boundary, such as 'dmz', 'internet-facing', 'guest', or 'public'. This attribute captures the actual network zone membership of the appliance's physical or logical adapters.
security_impact: The Rego rule network_binding_to_untrusted_interfaces evaluates this array in two conditions: when storage_protocol_bound_interfaces includes 'all' and this array is non-empty, and when management_interface_bound_to_all is true and this array is non-empty. A non-empty array means the device has a foothold in an untrusted zone, and any all-interface binding then exposes management or data protocols to that zone, enabling direct attack from hostile network segments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all network interfaces on the NAS and capture their IP addresses, then cross-reference against your network zone documentation to classify each interface. On Linux-based NAS platforms use ip addr or ifconfig.
how_to_obtain.command: ip addr show && ip route show && cat /proc/net/if_inet6 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each interface with its IP subnet. Map each subnet to your zone registry (e.g., 10.0.50.0/24 = DMZ). Any interface in a non-storage-VLAN zone should be added to this array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the network configuration section of the NAS management UI and review each configured adapter's IP assignment. Compare the subnet of each interface against your network segmentation diagram to identify DMZ, guest, or internet-facing subnets.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Synology: Control Panel > Network > Network Interface | QNAP: System > Network > TCP/IP | Generic: Management UI > System > Network Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each interface entry should show an IP and subnet. Any interface whose subnet falls outside the dedicated storage VLAN range should be classified as untrusted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the network or storage administrator to obtain the VLAN and zone assignments for each physical NIC port on the NAS chassis. Request the network diagram showing switch port VLAN membership for the NAS uplinks.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A zone-annotated list of all NAS network interfaces. If any interface lands in a DMZ, guest, public Wi-Fi, or internet-routable VLAN, the array should include that zone label.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run a network scan from hosts in each suspected zone to determine reachability of the NAS IP(s). Reachability from a DMZ or guest VLAN confirms an interface exists in that zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the NAS responds to pings or port scans from a non-storage VLAN host, that zone type should appear in untrusted_interface_types_present.

option_description: Controls whether the NAS appliance has chassis intrusion detection configured—either via hardware sensors (chassis-open microswitch) or software drive-presence monitoring—that generates an alert when the enclosure is physically opened or drives are removed without authorization. Alerts should be routed to a monitoring system or SIEM.
security_impact: The Rego rule physical_access_without_disk_lock_or_chassis_security fires when volume_encryption_enabled is false AND chassis_intrusion_detection_enabled is false. Without chassis intrusion detection, a physical attacker can silently remove drives and walk away with storage media. Even if drives are later discovered missing, the absence of a timestamped alert prevents forensic reconstruction of when the event occurred and which actor was on-site, eliminating accountability for physical data theft.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log into the NAS management interface and navigate to the hardware monitoring or notification section. Look for chassis sensor, drive removal alert, or physical security settings. On Synology check Control Panel > Notification and Hardware & Power > HDD/SSD. On QNAP check System > Hardware > General and the Notification Center.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Synology: Control Panel > Notification > Rules > Hardware Events | QNAP: Control Panel > Notification Center > System Events > Disk Removal
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An enabled alert rule for 'disk removal', 'chassis opened', or 'drive disconnected' events routed to email, SNMP trap, or syslog confirms this is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based NAS platforms, check if a chassis intrusion kernel module or smartmontools disk monitoring daemon is running and whether it has alert hooks configured.
how_to_obtain.command: lsmod | grep -i chassis; systemctl status smartd 2>/dev/null; cat /etc/smartd.conf 2>/dev/null | grep -i remove
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smartd running with drive removal directives (e.g., -n standby,q) and alert commands configured confirms software-based detection. Absence of any chassis module or smartd alert hooks means the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review system event logs for any historical chassis or drive removal events. If no such event categories exist in the log schema, the feature is not configured. Check for syslog entries with keywords related to disk hot-plug events.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of timestamped chassis or drive-removal log entries confirms the detection mechanism is active. A total absence of such event types in historical logs suggests the feature is disabled or unconfigured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Ask the NAS administrator whether chassis intrusion alerts have been tested and whether they are integrated with the SIEM or monitoring platform. Request evidence of a test alert (e.g., a SIEM ticket or email notification from a simulated drive removal).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A test alert record or SIEM event showing a drive-removal notification with timestamp confirms operational chassis intrusion detection. No evidence of testing should be treated as not effectively enabled.

typical_values: true (enterprise models with hardware sensors or configured smartd alerts)

option_description: Controls whether the NAS appliance requires an authentication challenge—such as administrator credentials entered via the management interface, a physical key lock, or an out-of-band confirmation—before permitting hot-removal of drives from the chassis. This prevents unauthorized personnel with physical access from extracting storage media while the system is running.
security_impact: The Rego rule physical_access_without_disk_lock_or_chassis_security fires when volume_encryption_enabled is false AND drive_hot_removal_authentication_required is false. Without drive removal authentication, any individual with physical access to the server room can pull drives from a running NAS and obtain all data without needing network credentials, bypassing all software-layer access controls. This is a direct data exfiltration path requiring no technical skill.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the NAS management console for drive lock or hot-swap authentication settings. On enterprise NAS platforms such as Synology SA series or QNAP enterprise models, look in Storage & Snapshots > Storage > Disk or in the hardware security settings for drive lock options.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Synology Enterprise: Storage Manager > HDD/SSD > Disk Lock | QNAP Enterprise: Storage & Snapshots > Storage > Disks > Disk Security | Generic: Management UI > Storage > Drive Security
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A 'Disk Lock' or 'Drive Removal Authentication' setting shown as enabled with a configured PIN or password confirms the attribute is true. Most consumer NAS models will not have this option at all, implying false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review vendor hardware specifications for the NAS model to determine whether drive hot-removal authentication is a supported feature. Consult the NAS administrator to verify whether physical key locks have been installed on drive bays and whether that constitutes an authentication requirement per policy.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vendor documentation confirming the feature exists combined with administrator confirmation it is enabled. For models where the feature does not exist in hardware, the attribute is false by default and compensating controls (volume encryption, physical cage locks) should be documented.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Synology NAS with DSM, use the synodiskpowerctl or synostorage CLI tools to check disk lock status if available. For QNAP use the QCLI tool.
how_to_obtain.command: synodiskpowerctl --get-lock-status 2>/dev/null || qcli --disk --get-lock 2>/dev/null || echo 'Command not supported on this model'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output indicating 'locked' or 'authentication required' confirms the feature is enabled. 'Command not found' or 'not supported' indicates the model does not support this feature and the attribute is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a physical security review of the NAS enclosure by visually inspecting drive bays for physical key locks or anti-tamper mechanisms. Verify with the facilities or security team that key custody procedures are documented if physical locks are the control.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Visible key lock cylinders in drive bays in the locked position, combined with documented key custody, is an acceptable physical control. Open drive bays with no locking mechanism means the attribute is false.

typical_values: false (default and most common, especially consumer/prosumer models)
true (enterprise NAS with disk lock feature enabled, or physical key locks installed)

option_description: Controls whether the NAS management interface and share authentication layer enforce automatic account lockout after a configurable number of consecutive failed login attempts. When enabled, accounts are temporarily or permanently locked following repeated failures, requiring administrator intervention or a cooldown period before further authentication attempts are permitted.
security_impact: The Rego rule absence_of_failed_login_lockout_or_rate_limiting fires when BOTH account_lockout_enabled is false AND rate_limiting_enabled is false. Without either control, the management interface and file-sharing endpoints accept an unlimited number of authentication attempts, making them fully susceptible to brute-force and password-spray attacks. Combined with management_interface_exposure of 'internet_facing' or 'internal', this creates a practical path to credential compromise on all local accounts including admin.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Synology DSM, navigate to Control Panel > Security > Account and locate the 'Enable account lockout' checkbox. Verify the lockout threshold (number of attempts) and lockout duration are set to policy-compliant values. On QNAP go to Control Panel > System Security > Account Access and check the brute-force protection settings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Synology: Control Panel > Security > Account > Account Lockout | QNAP: Control Panel > System > Security > Account Access Protection | Generic: Management UI > Security > Authentication Policy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Account lockout enabled with a threshold of 5 or fewer failed attempts and a lockout duration of at least 10 minutes represents a compliant configuration. Disabled or absent settings confirm account_lockout_enabled is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect PAM configuration files or the NAS-specific authentication policy configuration files to determine if pam_tally2, pam_faillock, or equivalent modules are configured with deny thresholds.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'auth required pam_faillock.so deny=5 unlock_time=600' confirm lockout is enforced at the OS level. Absence of deny directives means account_lockout_enabled is false at the system layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Synology DSM security policy via synosetkeyvalue or the Synology DSM configuration database for the account lockout parameters.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A key-value entry confirming lockout is enabled with a threshold value. Absence or a value of 'no'/'0' means account_lockout_enabled is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review authentication logs for evidence of lockout events. The presence of lockout-related log entries would confirm the feature has fired historically, indicating it is configured. Their total absence after reviewing auth logs with multiple failure sequences could indicate it is not enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'account.?lock|too many fail|locked out|authentication failure' /var/log/auth.log /var/log/secure /var/log/messages 2>/dev/null | tail -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing 'account locked' events after repeated failures confirm lockout is operational. This method alone is insufficient—lack of log entries does not confirm the setting is enabled if no lockout events have occurred.

typical_values: false (default on most NAS platforms without explicit hardening)
true (explicitly configured in security settings with defined threshold and duration)

option_description: Controls whether the NAS enforces rate limiting or auto-block mechanisms on authentication attempts to the management interface and share access endpoints. Rate limiting may include progressive delays between attempts, temporary IP-based blocking after threshold failure counts, or CAPTCHA challenges. This is a complementary control to account lockout that operates at the network/session layer rather than the account layer.
security_impact: The Rego rule absence_of_failed_login_lockout_or_rate_limiting fires only when BOTH account_lockout_enabled and rate_limiting_enabled are false. Either control alone satisfies the rule, but when neither is present, brute-force attacks can proceed at wire speed against all authentication endpoints. The rule also considers management_interface_exposure as contextual severity—internet-facing exposure with no rate limiting or lockout creates a critical-severity unauthenticated brute-force attack surface.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Synology DSM navigate to Control Panel > Security > Auto Block and verify it is enabled with a defined failure count threshold and block period. On QNAP navigate to Control Panel > System > Security > IP Access Protection and confirm rate limiting or auto-blocking is active for management and file services.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Synology: Control Panel > Security > Auto Block (enable, set attempts threshold and block period) | QNAP: Control Panel > System > Security > IP Access Protection | TrueNAS: System > Advanced > Login Attempts
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Auto Block enabled with 5 or fewer allowed failures within a 5-minute window, resulting in a block period of at least 30 minutes, represents a compliant rate-limiting configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the NAS auto-block or IP-deny configuration file. On Synology, the auto-block list and configuration are stored in /etc/synoautoblock.conf or managed via the security daemon.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A configuration file with enabled=yes and threshold/period values confirms rate limiting is configured. An empty or absent file, or enabled=no, means rate_limiting_enabled is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether fail2ban, sshguard, or an equivalent rate-limiting daemon is running on the NAS operating system, which would provide IP-level rate limiting for SSH and web management ports.
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl status fail2ban 2>/dev/null; systemctl status sshguard 2>/dev/null; fail2ban-client status 2>/dev/null | grep 'Jail list'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: fail2ban or sshguard running with active jails covering the management port and SSH confirms rate limiting is enabled. Neither service present or both stopped means rate_limiting_enabled depends entirely on any built-in NAS UI setting.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a controlled authentication rate test against the management interface from an authorized test host. Send 10 rapid consecutive failed login attempts and observe whether subsequent attempts are throttled, delayed, or result in a source IP block.
how_to_obtain.command: for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' -X POST https://<NAS_IP>:5001/webapi/auth.cgi -d 'api=SYNO.API.Auth&method=login&version=3&account=admin&passwd=wrongpass&session=FileStation&format=cookie'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Increasing response times (progressive delay) or HTTP 429 / connection refused responses after the threshold number of attempts confirm rate limiting is active. Consistent fast responses across all 10 attempts indicate rate_limiting_enabled is false.

typical_values: false (default on many NAS platforms, particularly older firmware versions)
true (explicitly enabled via Auto Block or IP Access Protection in management UI)
